observations: Bear It's rules plus a timed worker gate; rewards follow gates (S2-b, S4-a) or set the approach lane (S3-b).
Single landing boxes become a 10-box landing field after the big hole; its first box is where an angled-left jump lands.
Only 4 explosives in 42 boxes, each a key: TNT heading a line dictates order, a TNT forces a jump, a Nitro pair is a strip-wide hurdle.
Ice pairs return escalated (W+? from the left, then striped+? from the middle with instant hold-right).
Occlusion behind totems hides a ? and C3, the only hidden placement in the bear stages, flagged on the perfect page.
A 2x2 opening block banks 10% of the boxes before any hazard.
Density peaks in S2 (15); S3 is a deliberate calm (POINT 11) before the hidden-box forest.
The fruit trail can lead away from the box line (S3-c).
The live warp icon is a box-less hidden exit.
openQuestions: Plain icons identified only as non-?/non-striped are wood? (could be striped).
S1-a and S4-c lanes medium confidence.

geometryObservations: The title is the escalation axis, but tuned to the plain jump. Wide ponds (S1 POINT 2, S2 POINT 9) ask for the speed burst, yet F2 p097L says a normal jump from the very edge reaches. A 'big jump' sits at the plain jump's maximum range from the lip; the burst only widens the take-off window.

Almost every gap lands on something that matters: a ? (S1-b), a crate pair in one lane (S1-d), a crate field whose first box sits on the angled-left landing (S2-c), an island (POINT 13), the crystal strip, or the next slab gate (POINT 10, 14). The landing, not the width, is the design.

The new obstacle is a two-state gate read at speed. The worker slab is lowered (≈ 1 u, jump) or raised (≈ 2-2.5 u, ride under). Its seven appearances each add one coupling: alone and lowered (P7) → raised with a hole behind (P8) → raised on a pond's landing (P10) → lowered then an orca hole (P12) → orca hole then lowered (P14) → a double gate with a fake-out hold (P16) → raised as the final gate (P19).

Jump height becomes the advanced skill. Bear It always wanted full jumps; here POINT 4 (double narrow pond), POINT 10 (land early) and POINT 14 (small hops or 'bang your shins on the slab') make the SHORT jump correct. The gaps are shortened on purpose so a full jump overshoots into the next hazard.
Orca holes are deterministic side gates whose side is named and then flipped: left at holes 1-2 (teach by repetition), right at POINT 12 (flip), left again in S4. F2 states the side each time.

Ice patches return three times with rising stakes: with a W + ? pair entered from the left (S2), empty (S3, rehearsal with nothing to lose), and with a striped + ? pair entered at an angle with an instant hold (S4). The empty middle patch teaches without punishing.
Rest is declared, and density alternates. S1 opens with abundance (the 2×2 block) before any gap; POINT 11 tells the player to relax after the S2 peak; S2 and S4 are dense, S1 and S3 calmer.

Width is a difficulty dial. The road is ≈ 5-7 u through S3 and becomes a ≈ 2-3 u strip between ponds in S4, where two Nitro fill the whole width: lateral escape is removed exactly when the final jump chain starts.
The finale recombines every verb on one strip: plain break → Nitro hurdle (early jump) → wider break (dash-jump) → raised slab (no jump). Four different answers in a row (D2 s26-s28).

No enemy can be attacked on the bear. Workers, orcas and seals are gates and hurdles placed where a jump is already needed: in pits (orcas), across the road on a take-off or landing (workers), inside a crate field (seals).

Fruit lines time and mislead. D2 s12: take off as you pick up the last fruit before the big hole. At S3-c the fruit trail bends right round totems beside a water channel while the crate asks for a cut back left.
Totems change role four times: slalom posts (S1), a gate round a crate (S1-e), lying hurdles (S2), and an occluding forest that hides a crate and the checkpoint (S3).

Checkpoints sit on safe banks right before a new combination: C1 after the S1 pond, C2 beside the raised gate that ends S2, C3 inside the forest just before the double gate. The last section is short (9 crates) but holds the hardest chain.
geometryTransfer: Two-state bar gate. A horizontal `mover` bar that alternates between low (top ≈ 1.0 m: a full-charge ollie, apex ≈ 1.7 m, clears it) and high (underside ≥ 2.3 m: ride under). Teach it alone in the low state, then raised with a 3-4 m pit right behind it (duck, then ollie), then raised on the landing of a short pit (land short), then a low-high double with a long first hold.

'Big jump' tuned to lip range. At cruise (12 m/s) a full ollie carries ≈ 6.6 m; make the wide pit ≈ 6-6.5 m lip to lip so a lip ollie at cruise just makes it, and put a `speedpad` or a ≥ 20 m charge run-up before it for margin. Put the first crate of a two-line field 1-2 m past the landing lip, with a TNT heading the other line so the sweep order is fixed.

Short-jump traps. Two pits ≈ 2.3-3 m long with a ≈ 3 m strip between: a charged ollie (≥ 6.6 m) overshoots into the second pit, so a tap ollie (apex ≈ 0.56 m) or an uncharged hop is the answer. Measure the tap-ollie distance in the probe before relying on it.

Narrow-strip finale. A 2.3-3.5 m strip between pits holding: pit 1 (plain ollie), a Nitro pair spanning the strip (full-charge ollie clears one crate, 1.15 m, by ≈ 0.5 m; touch = death), pit 2 (needs charge), then a raised `mover` bar to ride under. Space the beats ≥ 6-7 m apart at cruise so each touchdown lasts ≈ 0.5 s.

Alternating side gate. A pit split into left and right halves with two `crusher` or `firetiki` hazards firing in alternation. Repeat the same safe side twice in the first section, flip it in the third, and put a crate on the take-off of the wrong side once the rule is known.
